t.1.32.1: Śaunaka said: The serpents, dear son, were born mighty and hard to approach. But then, having learned of that curse, what did they do next?
t.1.32.2: But of them, the blessed Śeṣa of great fame abandoned Kadrū and undertook vast austerity, living on air alone and keeping his vows restrained.
t.1.32.3: Reaching Gandhamādana, he devoted himself to austerities at Badarī, at Gokarṇa, in the Puṣkara forest, and likewise on the slope of Himavant.
t.1.32.4: At those various holy tīrthas and sacred shrines he dwelt, given to solitude, self-restrained, constantly master of his senses.
t.1.32.5: The Grandsire beheld that terrible austerity being performed, and him, the lord, his flesh, skin and sinews withered, wearing matted locks and garments of bark.
t.1.32.6: The Grandfather spoke to him, who was steadfast in truth and practising austerities: “What is this you are doing, Śeṣa? Work for the welfare of all creatures.”
t.1.32.8: Śeṣa said: All my brothers born of the same womb are dull-witted; I cannot bear to live with them, so may you, sir, grant your consent to this.
t.1.32.7: For with your fierce austerity, O sinless one, you are scorching the creatures. Tell me, Śeṣa, the wish that has long been lodged in your heart.
t.1.32.9: They constantly resent one another as if they were enemies. Therefore I practise austerities, so that I may not see them.
t.1.32.11: And they hate him exceedingly; yet he too is exceedingly mighty, by virtue of the boon granted by his father, the great-souled Kaśyapa.
t.1.32.10: They never cease to resent Vinatā and her son, yet Vainateya is another brother of ours, O Grandsire.
t.1.32.13: Brahmā said: I know, O Śeṣa, the conduct of all your brothers. And because of their mother's offence, too, a great danger indeed hangs over your brothers.
t.1.32.12: So I, having undertaken austerities, shall cast off this body, so that even in the state after death there may be no association for me with them.
t.1.32.14: O serpent, a remedy for this has already been provided beforehand for all your brothers; you should not grieve.
t.1.32.15: And choose from me a boon, Śeṣa, whatever is desired by you; for I wish to give you a boon today, since my delight in you is supreme.
t.1.32.16: Fortunately, O best of serpents, your mind is set upon dharma; and from now on may your mind remain even more firmly fixed in dharma.
t.1.32.17: Śeṣa said: This alone is the boon I desire today, O great-grandsire: may my mind delight in dharma, in tranquility, and in austerity, O lord.
t.1.32.18: Brahmā said: I am pleased with this self-restraint and tranquility of yours, Śeṣa. But at my command you must carry out this word of mine, which is for the welfare of the creatures.
t.1.32.19: O Śeṣa, take firm hold of this earth, furnished with mountains and forests, together with its oceans, its mines and its cities, which is quaking, and hold it properly and well, so that it may be steady.
t.1.32.20: Śeṣa said: As the god, the boon-giver Prajāpati, lord of the earth, lord of beings, lord of the world, has spoken, so shall I hold the earth steady and unmoving; place it upon my head, O Prajāpati.
t.1.32.21: Go beneath the earth, O best of serpents; she herself will grant you an opening. By your upholding this earth, O Śeṣa, a great kindness will have been done for me.
t.1.32.23: You are Śeṣa, O best of nāgas, the god of dharma, for you alone uphold this earth, embracing all of it with your endless coils, just as I do, or as the slayer of Bala does.
t.1.32.22: Saying “So be it,” the mighty lord, eldest-born of the foremost serpents, entered a cleft in the earth and, abiding there, bears upon his head this goddess Earth, whose rim is the ocean, holding her firmly on every side.
t.1.32.24: Thus the mighty serpent Ananta dwells beneath the earth, the powerful lord alone upholding the earth at the command of Brahmā.
t.1.32.25: And then the blessed Grandfather, highest of the immortals, gave Suparṇa, the son of Vinatā, to Ananta as his friend.
